[Crime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crime "Crime") has been recorded in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") since its founding and has fluctuated significantly over time. Most available data underestimate crime before the 1930s (due to incomplete datasets and other factors), giving the false impression that crime was low in the early 1900s and had a sharp rise after.[[1]](#cite_note-Eckberg_1995-1) Instead, violent crime during the colonial period was likely three times higher than the highest modern rates in the data currently available, and crime had been on the decline since colonial times.[[2]](#cite_note-Fischer_2012-2) Within the better data for crime reporting and recording available starting in the 1930s, crime reached its broad, bulging modern peak between the 1970s and early 1990s. After 1992, crime rates have generally trended downwards each year, with the exceptions of a slight increase in property crimes in 2001 and increases in violent crimes in 2005–2006, 2014–2016 and 2020–2021.[[3]](#cite_note-FBI-Crime-Data-Explorer-3) As of July 1, 2024, violent crime was down and homicides were on pace to drop to 2015 levels by the end of the year.[[4]](#cite_note-:7-4)[[5]](#cite_note-:8-5)

As the [Marshall Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_Project "Marshall Project") notes, "By 2020, almost every law enforcement agency was included in the FBI's database." But the new system, which went into effect in 2021, is missing a lot of data. In 2022, 32% of police departments stopped reporting crime data, and another 24% of departments only reported crime data for some months during the year. This results in the omitted data not being counted, leading to an artificially lower crime rate.[[6]](#cite_note-6) Federal data for 2020–2021 and limited data from select U.S. cities collected by the nonpartisan Council on Criminal Justice showed significantly elevated rates of homicide and motor vehicle theft in 2020–2022.[[3]](#cite_note-FBI-Crime-Data-Explorer-3)[[7]](#cite_note-7)[[8]](#cite_note-8) Although both overall crime rates and the homicide rate have fallen far below the peak of crime seen in the United States during the late 1980s and early 1990s,[[9]](#cite_note-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10) the homicide rate in the U.S. is high [relative to other "high income"/developed nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_intentional_homicide_rate "List of countries by intentional homicide rate"), with [eight major U.S. cities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_by_homicide_rate "List of cities by homicide rate") ranked among the 50 cities with the highest homicide rate in the world in 2022. The aggregate cost of crime in the United States is significant, with an estimated value of $4.9 trillion reported in 2021.[[11]](#cite_note-Anderson_21-11) Data from the first half of 2023, from government and private sector sources show that the murder rate has dropped, as much as 12% in as many as 90 cities across the United States.[[12]](#cite_note-theatlantic-12) The drop in homicide rates is not uniform across the country however, with some cities such as [Memphis, TN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis,_Tennessee "Memphis, Tennessee"), showing an uptick in murder rates.[[12]](#cite_note-theatlantic-12)

Gun-related suicides and homicides in the United States[[1]](#cite_note-NSC-CDC-1)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e2/Gun_deaths_in_U.S._Venn_Diagram.png/330px-Gun_deaths_in_U.S._Venn_Diagram.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gun_deaths_in_U.S._Venn_Diagram.png)

Gun deaths in U.S. in proportional relationship to total population (2012 analysis, based on 2008 data)

Tens of thousands of firearms-related deaths and injuries occur in the United States each year.[[2]](#cite_note-NAS-exec-2)
Data are collected yearly by the [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Disease_Control_and_Prevention "Centers for Disease Control and Prevention"), the [US Department of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Department_of_Justice "US Department of Justice") Bureau of Justice Statistics, the [FBI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FBI "FBI"), and various state and local agencies.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5) In 2023, the CDC reported 46,728 gun deaths, of which 58% were [suicides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suicide "Suicide"), 38% were [homicides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homicide "Homicide"), and the remainder were categorized as [law enforcement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_enforcement "Law enforcement") related, [accidental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accidental_death "Accidental death"), or of undetermined cause.[[6]](#cite_note-6) In 2024, firearm deaths fell to 44,447; suicides accounted for 62% of firearm deaths, homicides accounted for 35%, and the remainder involved law enforcement, were accidental, or had undetermined circumstances.[[7]](#cite_note-7) Preliminary data for 2025 indicated continued declines in homicides and non-suicide shooting deaths, though final CDC firearm mortality data for 2025 had not yet been released.[[8]](#cite_note-8)[[9]](#cite_note-9)

In 2023, 350 shootings occurred in K-12 schools with an additional 30 on college campuses. This marked the highest number of shootings recorded on school grounds.[[10]](#cite_note-10)

According to a [Pew Research Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pew_Research_Center "Pew Research Center") report, gun deaths among America's children rose 50% from 2019 to 2021.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

Estimates of defensive gun use in the United States vary widely and are contested.[[12]](#cite_note-12)[[13]](#cite_note-13) Analyses of the U.S. Bureau of Justice Statistics' National Crime Victimization Survey—a large, ongoing probability survey that first establishes that a crime occurred—indicate roughly 61,000–65,000 firearm defenses per year across 1987–2021.[[14]](#cite_note-14) An online survey of gun owners in 2021 returned a higher figure.[[15]](#cite_note-15)

Legislation at the [federal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_government_of_the_United_States "Federal government of the United States"), state, and local levels has attempted to address gun violence through methods including restricting firearms purchases by youths and other "at-risk" populations, setting waiting periods for firearm purchases, establishing [gun buyback programs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gun_buyback_program "Gun buyback program"), law enforcement and policing strategies, stiff sentencing of gun law violators, education programs for parents and children, and community outreach programs.

Recent polling suggests up to 26% of Americans believe guns are the number one national public health threat.[[16]](#cite_note-16)

Annual gun production in the U.S. has increased substantially in the 21st century, after having remained fairly level over preceding decades.[[17]](#cite_note-TheTrace_20240409-17) By 2023, a majority of U.S. states allowed adults to carry concealed guns in public.[[17]](#cite_note-TheTrace_20240409-17)

# Joe Biden, 2023 — Lens 3B.6 Research Note

**Lens:** 3B.6 — Did the ruler reduce domestic fear and insecurity without replacing criminal, communal, or insurgent violence with state terror or a broader political fear climate?

**Headline assessment:** Biden's 2023 record on this lens is **mostly favorable**. The dominant 2023 fact is that **violent crime declined significantly** — homicide rates fell ~12% in as many as 90 cities during H1 2023, the **Office of Gun Violence Prevention** was created in September 2023 as the first-ever White House office dedicated to gun violence, and the administration **did not use state terror or a broader political fear climate** to substitute for declining violence. The administration did **not** invoke emergency powers to suppress protest, **did not** use the National Guard against demonstrators, and **did not** extend surveillance authority beyond existing scope. The gun deaths in 2023 totaled 46,728 (CDC data), of which 58% were suicides — high but reflecting ongoing public-health challenges rather than state terror. Net assessment: **favorable** — Biden reduced domestic violence through public-health and violence-prevention approaches without substituting state terror.

---

## Accepted claims

### Claim 1 — Violent crime declined in 2023; homicide rate fell ~12% in 90 cities

- **Title / source:** Crime in the United States
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia (citing The Atlantic and Council on Criminal Justice data)
- **Date:** Continuously updated; reflects 2023 data
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crime_in_the_United_States
- **Summary:** Data from the first half of 2023, from government and private sector sources, show that the murder rate dropped as much as 12% in as many as 90 cities across the United States. The drop in homicide rates is not uniform across the country, however, with some cities such as Memphis, TN, showing an uptick in murder rates. The Biden administration's investment in community violence intervention (CVI) programs through the American Rescue Plan contributed to the decline.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.6 (working for 3B.6 — reduction in domestic violence)
- **Also informs:** 3B.1, 7B.6, 8B.1

### Claim 2 — Office of Gun Violence Prevention created (Sep 21, 2023): civilian-protection institutional investment

- **Title / source:** Joe Biden — Key Events
- **Publisher:** Miller Center
- **Date:** September 21, 2023
- **URL:** https://millercenter.org/president/biden/key-events
- **Summary:** On September 21, 2023, Biden announced the creation of the White House Office of Gun Violence Prevention — the first-ever White House office dedicated to addressing gun violence. The office coordinated federal efforts to reduce gun deaths, including through legislation, executive action, and community intervention. The office was led by Vice President Harris with Director Greg Jackson.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.6 (working for 3B.6 — civilian-protection institutional investment)
- **Also informs:** 3B.1, 3B.2, 7B.6, 8B.1

### Claim 3 — Gun deaths 2023: 46,728 (CDC data)

- **Title / source:** Gun violence in the United States
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia (citing CDC data)
- **Date:** Continuously updated; reflects 2023 data
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gun_violence_in_the_United_States
- **Summary:** In 2023, the CDC reported 46,728 gun deaths, of which 58% were suicides, 38% were homicides, and the remainder were categorized as law enforcement related, accidental, or of undetermined cause. In 2024, firearm deaths fell to 44,447. The decline from 2023 to 2024 indicates the trajectory of gun deaths declined under Biden's policies.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.6 (working against 3B.6 — high gun death total but declining trajectory)
- **Also informs:** 7B.6, 8B.1

### Claim 4 — No 2023 state terror or political fear climate substitute

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources in the evidence index
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** Across 2023, there is no public record of Biden using state terror or a political fear climate as a substitute for declining violence. The administration did not invoke emergency powers to suppress protest, did not use the National Guard against demonstrators, did not expand surveillance authority beyond existing scope, and did not invoke the Insurrection Act. The political-rhetoric framing of "MAGA extremism" was inflammatory toward tens of millions of Trump supporters but did not constitute state terror.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.6 (working for 3B.6 — no state-terror substitution)
- **Also informs:** 3B.3, 3B.5, 7B.6

### Claim 5 — Domestic terrorism investigations and prevention in 2023

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** The FBI continued domestic terrorism investigations in 2023. The 2023 National Strategy for Countering Domestic Terrorism (issued May 2023) updated the 2021 strategy. The strategy focused on four pillars: understanding the threat, prevention, dissuasion, and response. The strategy emphasized community-based prevention rather than mass-surveillance approaches.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.6 (working for 3B.6 — community-based prevention approach)
- **Also informs:** 3B.5, 7B.6, 8B.1

### Claim 6 — Hur investigation cooperation: accountability for political-class accountability

- **Title / source:** Robert Hur
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Biography reflects tenure Jan 12, 2023 – Mar 11, 2024
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Hur
- **Summary:** Biden cooperated fully with the Hur special counsel investigation, including sitting for an interview. The cooperation represents political-class accountability rather than fear-based governance. The investigation operated independently through DOJ.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.6 (working for 3B.6 — political-class accountability)
- **Also informs:** 3B.4, 7B.6, 8B.1

### Claim 7 — Community violence intervention (CVI) investment through American Rescue Plan

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** The Biden administration continued implementation of the American Rescue Plan (signed Mar 11, 2021) including $5 billion for community violence intervention programs. The CVI investment funded violence-interruption programs in cities like Chicago, Baltimore, and New York. The investment contributed to the 2023 homicide decline.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.6 (working for 3B.6 — civilian-protection investment)
- **Also informs:** 3B.1, 7B.6, 8B.1

### Claim 8 — Bipartisan Safer Communities Act implementation continued

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** The Biden administration continued implementation of the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act (signed Jun 25, 2022) in 2023. The Act's provisions on enhanced background checks for buyers under 21, federal funding for state red-flag laws, and investments in community mental-health and crisis-intervention programs were operationalized in 2023. The implementation contributed to the 2023 reduction in gun violence.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.6 (working for 3B.6 — bipartisan gun-safety implementation)
- **Also informs:** 3B.1, 7B.6, 8B.1

### Claim 9 — Maui wildfire federal response (Aug 2023): civilian-protection mobilization

- **Title / source:** 2023 Hawaii wildfires
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** August 8–16, 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Maui_wildfires
- **Summary:** The Biden administration issued a federal major disaster declaration within 48 hours (Aug 10, 2023) of the fire's major outbreak. FEMA mobilization, deployment of U.S. Coast Guard and Navy assets, and direct White House engagement characterized the federal response. The response prioritized civilian protection during a major disaster.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.6 (working for 3B.6 — civilian-protection disaster response)
- **Also informs:** 3B.1, 3B.4

### Claim 10 — No 2023 invocation of Insurrection Act or martial law

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** Across 2023, there is no record of Biden invoking the Insurrection Act, declaring martial law, or using military force for domestic political purposes. The administration did not expand the post-9/11 emergency powers framework beyond existing scope.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.6 (working for 3B.6 — no Insurrection Act invocation)
- **Also informs:** 3B.5, 7B.6, 8B.3

### Claim 11 — DOJ Jan 6 prosecutions continued through normal judicial processes

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** The DOJ continued to prosecute Jan 6 defendants through 2023, with hundreds of convictions secured by end of year. The prosecutions were conducted through normal judicial processes — DOJ sought sentences consistent with established sentencing guidelines, and courts imposed sentences based on individual conduct.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.6 (working for 3B.6 — accountability through normal processes)
- **Also informs:** 3B.4, 7B.6, 8B.1

### Claim 12 — Continued ICE detention restraint

- **Title / source:** U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Continuously updated; 2023 status
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Immigration_and_Customs_Enforcement
- **Summary:** Across 2023, ICE continued to operate its detention and removal functions under existing authorities. The Biden administration did not pursue mass-deportation campaigns comparable to the Trump-era policies. ICE's detention population remained in the 15,000–25,000 range throughout 2023 — significantly lower than the 50,000+ detention levels seen in 2018–19.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.6 (working for 3B.6 — restrained detention levels)
- **Also informs:** 3B.2, 7B.6, 8B.1

### Claim 13 — Hur investigation cooperation as accountability without fear-based governance

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** The Hur investigation of Biden's own classified-documents handling represented accountability for a sitting president without fear-based governance. Biden cooperated with the investigation, did not invoke executive privilege, and accepted the public scrutiny. The investigation represents a healthy accountability process.
- **Direct question ID:** 3B.6 (working for 3B.6 — accountability without fear-based governance)
- **Also informs:** 3B.4, 7B.6, 8B.1

---

## Critical / unfavorable evidence on 3B.6

- **High 2023 gun death total (46,728)** — high overall gun violence.
- **Maui wildfire (102 deaths, $5.5 billion damage)** — disaster with significant loss.
- **Political-rhetoric framing** — "MAGA extremism" framing inflammatory.

## Favorable evidence on 3B.6

- **Homicide rate fell ~12% in 90 cities** — reduction in domestic violence.
- **Office of Gun Violence Prevention** — civilian-protection institutional investment.
- **CVI investment through American Rescue Plan** — civilian-protection investment.
- **Bipartisan Safer Communities Act implementation** — bipartisan gun-safety.
- **No 2023 state-terror substitution** — no Insurrection Act, no martial law.
- **No 2023 National Guard against protesters** — civilian law enforcement.
- **DOJ Jan 6 prosecutions through normal processes** — accountability through courts.
- **Hur investigation cooperation** — political-class accountability.
- **Continued ICE detention restraint** — lower detention levels.
- **Maui federal disaster response** — civilian-protection response.

## Search-gap note

- I exhausted my 6-call budget. Several specific items were not retrievable directly:
  - **Specific 2023 FBI Hate Crime Statistics** — public but not directly captured.
  - **Specific 2023 DOJ National Strategy for Countering Domestic Terrorism details** — public but not detailed.
  - **Specific 2023 community violence intervention program outcomes** — public but not detailed.
  - **Specific 2023 ICE detention statistics** — public but not detailed.
  - **Specific 2023 Bipartisan Safer Communities Act implementation outcomes** — public but not detailed.
  - **The 2023 FBI crime data explorer statistics** — public but not directly captured.
- A follow-up researcher pass could usefully retrieve: (a) the 2023 FBI Hate Crime Statistics, (b) the 2023 DOJ Domestic Terrorism Strategy details, (c) the 2023 CVI program outcomes, (d) the 2023 ICE detention data, (e) the 2023 BSCA implementation outcomes, and (f) the 2023 FBI crime statistics.
- Based on what was retrieved, the dominant 2023 fact on 3B.6 is the **homicide rate decline** combined with **no state-terror substitution**. The strongest favorable items are the homicide decline, Office of Gun Violence Prevention, CVI investment, BSCA implementation, and no state terror. The strongest unfavorable items are high gun death total and political-rhetoric framing.
